blocks.text: The chapter opens by naming readers across Pontus, Galatia, Cappadocia, Asia, and Bithynia, then offers a single blessing that joins new birth, living hope, resurrection, and an enduring inheritance. This promise of durable belonging stands alongside—not in denial of—the readers’ present trials. The later call to holiness grounds all of life in the scriptural declaration that God is holy.

sections.title: Reading the Address and Trials Carefully

blocks.text: “Elect sojourners of the Dispersion” may combine actual geographic scattering, a socially marginal identity, and Israel-shaped language; it does not by itself establish either the readers’ ethnicity or legal status. The letter’s references to former conduct may suggest substantial gentile presence, but they do not settle the audience’s precise makeup. Likewise, “foreknowledge” in the greeting should not be made to carry later systems of predestination, and the fire image for tested faith is a refining metaphor, not a reason to glorify suffering, manufacture persecution, or discourage safety.

Several of the chapter’s powerful images require careful reading. The command to be holy invokes Israel’s scriptures and calls for whole conduct before God; it should not be used to impose shame, exclusion, or coercive purity standards. The language of redemption by Christ’s precious blood evokes costly liberation and sacrificial imagery, but the phrase alone does not settle every account of how atonement works. Similarly, being born through imperishable seed and God’s enduring word describes communal new birth, not biological, racial, or nationalist descent.

The material that follows develops this opening within a coherent letter that combines blessing, ethical instruction, interpretation of Scripture, household discourse, and consolation shaped by hope for God’s future. Reading chapter 1 as the letter’s opening helps explain why its assurance, exhortation, and scriptural language remain closely intertwined.
